title: Faroe Islands Subsea Loop: Eighteen Islands, Six Tunnels

bestPeriod.window: May to September for open roads, ferries and puffins; late September for autumn light; winter driving is feasible but daylight is short and mountain roads close in gales

food.note: €55-90 per day; heimablídni home dinners €70-110 pp

transport.note: €400-600: flights, car hire €70-95 per day, tunnel tolls, inter-island ferries

activities.note: €100-200: Vestmanna bird cliffs boat, Kalsoy ferry and lighthouse hike fee, museums

summary: A seven-day road trips & scenic drive itinerary in Streymoy, Eysturoy, Norðoyar, Sandoy, Vágar, Faroe Islands.

itinerary.title: Vágar: Gásadalur and the western edge
itinerary.morning: Land at Vágar, collect the car. Drive first to Bøur, a village of turf roofs facing the sea stacks of Tindhólmur.
itinerary.afternoon: Through the old single-lane tunnel, or the new one, to Gásadalur, a village of sixteen people that had no road access until 2004; the postman used to walk over the mountain three times a week. The Múlafossur waterfall drops straight off the cliff beside it into the Atlantic.
itinerary.evening: Sørvágur or Miðvágur for the night. Buy food; shops close early and are shut on Sundays.

itinerary.title: Streymoy: Saksun, Tjørnuvík and the old high road
itinerary.morning: Take the Oyggjarvegur, the old mountain road over Streymoy, rather than the tunnel, it climbs into cloud with the whole island beneath it.
itinerary.afternoon: Saksun: a turf-roofed church, a tidal lagoon that empties completely at low water, and a handful of farms in an amphitheatre of cliffs. Then across to Tjørnuvík on the north coast, facing the Risin og Kellingin sea stacks, the giant and the witch, petrified while trying to drag the Faroes to Iceland.
itinerary.evening: Drive to Tórshavn. Walk Tinganes, the peninsula of red turf-roofed government buildings where the Løgting has met since Viking times, arguably the oldest continuous parliamentary site in the world.

itinerary.title: Eysturoy: Gjógv, Funningur and the pass
itinerary.morning: Through the Eysturoy subsea tunnel, past the illuminated undersea roundabout with its light installation and jellyfish sculpture. North to Funningur, said to be the first Norse settlement in the islands.
itinerary.afternoon: The Eiðisskarð pass beneath Slættaratindur (882 m, the highest point), then Gjógv, built around a 200 m natural sea gorge that served as its harbour.
itinerary.evening: Stay in Gjógv. There is one guesthouse, no restaurant, and complete silence.

itinerary.title: Norðoyar: Klaksvík, Viðareiði and Kalsoy
itinerary.morning: The Norðoya tunnel to Klaksvík, the second town and the fishing capital, with the extraordinary Christianskirkjan, a modern church with a Viking longhouse form and a rowing boat hung from the ceiling.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive to Viðareiði, the northernmost settlement, under Enniberg, one of the highest sea cliffs in Europe at 754 m. Alternatively take the small ferry from Klaksvík to Kalsoy and drive its chain of single-lane tunnels to Trøllanes for the Kallur lighthouse walk, the most photographed ridge in the Faroes. Ferry capacity is tiny; queue early. `verify: true`
itinerary.evening: Klaksvík. The town brewery is a national institution.

itinerary.title: Vestmanna bird cliffs and Sandoy
itinerary.morning: The Vestmanna sea-cliff boat trip: two hours through sea caves and under 600 m cliffs stacked with guillemots, fulmars and puffins. It cancels in swell, so treat it as first-choice-if-calm.
itinerary.afternoon: Through the new Sandoy tunnel to Sandoy, sand dunes, the village of Skopun, and Húsavík with its medieval ruins. Sandoy is where Faroese people go when they want to be somewhere quiet, which tells you something.

itinerary.title: Tórshavn, Kirkjubøur and a home dinner
itinerary.morning: Kirkjubøur, the medieval episcopal seat: the roofless Gothic Magnus Cathedral begun around 1300, the small St Olav's church still in use, and Kirkjubøargarður, a farmhouse continuously inhabited for centuries.
itinerary.afternoon: Tórshavn properly, the National Museum, the Nordic House, the old town's black tarred houses with grass roofs, and the harbour.
itinerary.evening: Book a **heimablídni**: dinner in a Faroese family's home, several courses of lamb, fish and rhubarb, with the family eating alongside you. It is the single best thing you can do in the islands.

itinerary.title: Trøllkonufingur, Sørvágsvatn or Mykines, then out
itinerary.morning: Depending on wind: the Mykines boat for puffins, or the short walk to the Trælanípa cliff over Sørvágsvatn.
itinerary.afternoon: Fly out from Vágar. Allow generous slack for weather.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Føroyar or Hotel Brandan
accommodationStrategy.description: Two contrasting bases in the capital: Føroyar is turf-roofed on the hill with the harbour view; Brandan is newer, in town, with a spa. Both have secure parking, which matters more than it sounds in a place where the wind removes car doors.

accommodationStrategy.name: Gjáargarður
accommodationStrategy.description: The guesthouse at the gorge village, with home-cooked dinners booked at check-in. Essential for Day 3 because the alternative is an hour's drive back to Tórshavn on a mountain road in the dark.

accommodationStrategy.name: Klaksvík guesthouses
accommodationStrategy.description: Simple, cheap, and positioned so that the Kalsoy ferry and the Viðareiði drive both start from your door rather than 90 minutes away. Book the ferry morning and stay the night before, this is the sequencing that makes Day 4 work.

logistics.emergency: 112. The national hospital is in Tórshavn with smaller facilities in Klaksvík and Suðuroy. Helicopter evacuation is available and used.
logistics.weather: Wind, not rain, drives the itinerary. Above 15 m/s, mountain roads and ferries stop. Build two flexible days into seven and reorder daily around the forecast rather than fighting it.
logistics.bookingWindows: Cars: 2-3 months for summer. Heimablídni dinners: 3-6 weeks. Vestmanna boats: a few days, but expect cancellation. Guesthouses in Gjógv and Viðareiði: 2-3 months.

other.label: Tunnel tolls
other.text: The Vágar, Eysturoy and Sandoy subsea tunnels are tolled by automatic plate recognition and billed to the rental company, typically with an administration fee. Expect a bill after you get home. `verify: true`

other.label: Single-lane tunnels
other.text: Several older mountain tunnels, notably on Kalsoy and in the outer islands, are one lane with passing bays (marked **M**). The rule: the vehicle with the bay on its side pulls in. They are unlit, wet, and rock-walled. Drive slowly with headlights on.

other.label: Sheep
other.text: There are more sheep than people and they own the roads. Hitting one makes you liable to the owner. Assume a sheep behind every blind crest.

other.label: Ferries
other.text: Strandfaraskip Landsins runs the inter-island ferries; the Kalsoy and Mykines routes have small capacity and fill in summer. The Suðuroy ferry (2 h) is large and reliable. `verify: true`

other.label: Sundays
other.text: Shops, most restaurants and many attractions close. Fuel stations are largely automated. Plan food on Saturday.

proTips: Always take the **old mountain road** where one exists beside a tunnel. The Oyggjarvegur, the Norðradalsskarð and the Eiðisskarð are the three best drives in the North Atlantic and everyone else is underground.
Check **wind, not rain**. A Faroese 4 mm rain day with 6 m/s wind is a great day out; a dry day at 18 m/s is not.

The **Faroese helicopter** service links remote villages at subsidised fares and is one of Europe's great transport oddities. Seat release is scheduled and tourists may be limited to one-way sectors, check the current rules well ahead. `verify: true`
Fill the tank whenever you are below half. Fuel stations outside Tórshavn, Klaksvík and Vágar are sparse and several are card-only automats.

Photograph Saksun and Gásadalur **before 09:00 or after 20:00**. Both are tiny private settlements where residents have had real problems with visitor volume, arrive early, stay on marked paths, park only in the designated areas.
If a storm eats a day, the Nordic House, the National Museum and the Tórshavn swimming baths absorb it well, and a storm-day heimablídni is better than a calm-day one.

raw.driving_character: Short legs on excellent tarmac, punctuated by subsea tunnels, single-lane mountain tunnels with passing bays, and hairpin descents into fjord villages
raw.mountain_passes: The old Oyggjarvegur high road over Streymoy, the Eiðisskarð pass on Eysturoy, and the Norðradalsskarð, all worth taking instead of the tunnel
raw.tunnels: Vágatunnilin (2002), Norðoyatunnilin (2006), Eysturoyartunnilin (2020, with the world's only undersea roundabout), Sandoyartunnilin (2023)
raw.cross_border_rules: The Faroes are outside the EU and the Schengen customs union though within the Nordic passport area; hire cars cannot leave the archipelago
